name: Endpoint Patching & EDR Alerts

quiz.text: What does EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) primarily monitor?

answers.text: Only known virus signatures
Process behavior and suspicious activity patterns
Network bandwidth usage
User login times

quiz.text: In Alice's case, what was the direct consequence of leaving patch KB5035853 uninstalled for 3 days? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: The malicious macro was able to briefly access credential memory before EDR killed it
Suspicious login attempts were detected from a foreign IP address
The computer was permanently damaged
Alice's credentials had to be force-reset

quiz.text: What should you do when you receive an EDR alert that says a threat was 'partially blocked'?

answers.text: Ignore it since EDR handled the threat automatically
Review the alert details, install pending patches via Windows Settings, and report the incident
Immediately shut down your computer and leave it off
Delete the EDR software to stop the alerts

quiz.text: Which of the following are behavioral indicators that EDR systems look for? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Processes attempting to access credential storage (LSASS)
Hidden PowerShell processes spawning from documents
Normal web browsing activity
Unexpected network connections to unknown servers

quiz.text: Where should you install operating system security patches?

answers.text: Through the EDR portal's install button
Through Windows Settings > Windows Update
By downloading patches from external websites
Patches install themselves automatically and require no action

quiz.text: Why should you report an EDR alert even when the threat was successfully blocked? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: The security team can investigate if others received similar attacks
It helps improve defenses against future attacks
Reporting is required to unlock your computer
Other employees can be warned about the threat

steps.name: Introduction
steps.description: Today, you will learn how Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) systems monitor your workstation for threats - and what to do when they detect something suspicious.

steps.name: A Routine Thursday
steps.note: EDR systems continuously monitor endpoints for malicious activity. When they detect something suspicious, they alert both the user and the security team.
steps.description:
It's Thursday afternoon. Alice is finishing up a quarterly analysis report when an unusual notification catches her eye in the system tray.

A small shield icon is flashing amber - the company's EDR agent is trying to get her attention.
steps.instructions: Click Next to see the EDR alert.

steps.name: The EDR Alert

data.title: Sentinel Shield EDR
data.message:
Suspicious process behavior detected on ALICE-WS-2847.
Severity: High | Status: Partially Blocked: Immediate Action Required

steps.description: Here is what the EDR alert means: Sentinel Shield EDR - Alert Severity: High Type: Suspicious Process Behavior Details: A process attempted to access sensitive memory regions. This behavior pattern is associated with credential harvesting tools. Status: Partially Blocked: Immediate Action Required Recommended: Review alert details, install pending security update, and report incident.
steps.instructions: Click 'View Details' on the EDR notification to open the portal.

steps.name: Logging into the EDR Portal
steps.note: EDR systems use behavioral analysis to detect threats, even zero-day attacks that traditional antivirus might miss. When you see an EDR notification, always click 'View Details' to review the full alert.
steps.description: Clicking 'View Details' opened the Sentinel Shield EDR portal in Alice's browser. She needs to log in to review the full alert details and her endpoint's protection status.
steps.instructions: Log in to the EDR portal using the password manager.

steps.name: The EDR Dashboard
steps.note: A 'Partially Blocked' status means EDR stopped the attack, but not before some damage occurred. The missing patch was the gap the attacker exploited.

highlighterTexts: The dashboard shows 1 threat detected today. This is the alert triggered by the malicious macro in the spreadsheet Alice opened.
1 update has been pending for 3 days. This missing patch is the gap that allowed the attacker partial access before EDR could stop the process.
The alert badge says 'Partially Blocked', not fully blocked. This means EDR stopped the threat, but not before some damage was done. The severity is High.
Click 'View Alert Details' to see exactly what happened and how credentials may have been exposed.

steps.description:
The EDR portal dashboard shows Alice's workstation status at a glance: Endpoint Status: Protected
  • Last Scan: Today, 2:30 PM
  • Threat Detected: 1 (Today), Partially Blocked
  • Agent Version: 8.2.1 (Current)
Patch Status: 1 Update Pending
  • Critical Security Update KB5035853 available
  • Pending since: 3 days ago
Alice notices the alert status says "Partially Blocked", not fully blocked. The missing security update gave the attacker a brief window of access.
steps.instructions: Review the dashboard, then click 'View Alert Details'.

steps.name: Alert Details

highlighterTexts: The status is 'Partially Blocked': EDR terminated the malicious process, but not before it partially executed. The source was Q3_Budget_Summary.xlsm, a macro-enabled spreadsheet Alice opened from an email.
These are the suspicious behaviors EDR detected. Accessing LSASS memory means the attacker tried to steal stored passwords. Hidden PowerShell and outbound connections are classic signs of malware.
This is the critical detail: the malicious process accessed credential memory for about 4 seconds before EDR killed it. That was enough time to potentially harvest cached passwords.
This happened because vulnerability CVE-2024-26169 was unpatched. The missing update KB5035853 would have stopped the macro's process from elevating to SYSTEM and reaching credential memory.

steps.description:
The alert details reveal what happened: Alert ID: EDR-2024-847291 Detection Time: Today, 2:47 PM Status: Partially Blocked Process: svchost_update.exe (Suspicious name mimicking legitimate process) Source: Downloaded file: "Q3_Budget_Summary.xlsm" macro execution Behavioral Indicators:
  • Attempted to access LSASS memory (credential storage)
  • Spawned hidden PowerShell process
  • Attempted network connection to unknown external IP
Action Taken: Process terminated after partial execution: credentials may have been exposed Alice feels a chill. The process wasn't just blocked: it ran long enough to potentially harvest her credentials before EDR killed it.
steps.instructions: Review the alert details, then click 'Check Patch Status'.

steps.name: Patch Status Review
steps.note: EDR portals show you what needs to be patched, but the actual installation happens through your operating system's update settings, not through the EDR portal itself.
steps.description:
The patch status page shows: Operating System Patches:
  • KB5035853 (Critical Security Update): PENDING, 3 days
  • KB5034123 (Feature Update): Installed
  • KB5033891 (Security Update): Installed
The pending critical update (KB5035853) patches vulnerability CVE-2024-26169, a Windows Error Reporting Service flaw that lets code already running as a normal user elevate itself to SYSTEM: the exact privilege escalation used in today's attack once the macro ran. Because this patch was pending for 3 days, the vulnerability was open when the attacker struck. EDR caught the malicious behavior, but the missing patch is why credentials were partially exposed. Alice notices there is no install button here: EDR monitors patch status, but patches are installed through Windows Settings.
steps.instructions: Review the patch status page, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Consequences
steps.note: This is the real-world consequence of delayed patching. EDR stopped the process, but the 4-second window was enough for the attacker to harvest credentials and begin using them.

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Suspicious Activity Alert

We have detected multiple login attempts on your Stormveil Data account from an unrecognized IP address (185.234.xx.xx, Eastern Europe) within the last 15 minutes.

Our investigation indicates this may be related to the EDR alert on your workstation. The malicious process was able to briefly access credential memory before the EDR terminated it.

Immediate actions required:
  • Install the pending security update KB5035853 via Windows Settings > Windows Update
  • Report the full incident through the EDR portal
  • Do not share any credentials until our investigation is complete
We have temporarily blocked the suspicious IP and are monitoring your account. Your credentials will be force-reset as a precaution after the investigation.

IT Security Team
email.subject: URGENT: Suspicious Login Attempts on Your Account

highlighterTexts: Suspicious login attempts from Eastern Europe: the attacker is already trying to use Alice's compromised credentials. The 4-second window was enough.
IT Security instructs Alice to install the pending patch via Windows Settings and report the incident through the EDR portal.

steps.description:
While Alice is reviewing the patch information, a new email arrives. The subject line makes her stomach drop.

IT Security has detected suspicious login attempts on her account from an unrecognized IP address in Eastern Europe, within the last 15 minutes. The credential exposure from the EDR alert wasn't theoretical: someone is already trying to use her compromised credentials.
steps.instructions: Read the urgent email from IT Security.

answers.text: The EDR software was outdated and couldn't fully detect the threat
answers.explanation: The EDR agent was up to date (v8.2.1). The issue was a missing OS patch, not an EDR problem.

answers.text: A missing OS patch left a vulnerability open, allowing the malicious process to partially execute before EDR killed it
answers.explanation: The pending patch KB5035853 (3 days overdue) left vulnerability CVE-2024-26169 open. The macro started the process, and that unpatched flaw let it elevate to SYSTEM and read credential memory for ~4 seconds before EDR's behavioral analysis terminated it.

answers.text: Alice clicked 'Allow' on the EDR prompt, letting the process run
answers.explanation: EDR acts automatically based on behavioral analysis: it doesn't ask users whether to allow suspicious processes.

answers.text: The attacker disabled EDR before running the malicious process
answers.explanation: EDR was running and detected the threat. The problem was a vulnerability that existed before EDR could intervene.

data.question: Why was the EDR alert marked as 'Partially Blocked' instead of fully blocked?

answers.text: Shut down the computer immediately and wait for IT to fix it
answers.explanation: Shutting down doesn't address the root cause: the missing patch. IT Security specifically asked Alice to install the update and report the incident.

answers.text: Install the pending security update via Windows Settings, then report the incident through the EDR portal
answers.explanation: IT Security's email gave clear instructions: install the patch via Windows Settings to close the vulnerability, then report the full incident so the security team can investigate and protect other employees.

answers.text: Reply to the IT Security email with her current password so they can reset it faster
answers.explanation: Never share passwords via email, even with IT Security. Legitimate IT teams will never ask for your password. They can force-reset it server-side.

answers.text: Delete the Q3_Budget_Summary.xlsm file and continue working normally
answers.explanation: Deleting the file doesn't close the vulnerability or address the credential compromise. The missing patch and incident report are the priorities.

steps.name: Installing the Patch
steps.note: Security updates are installed via Windows Settings > Windows Update. EDR monitors your patch status but the actual patching happens at the OS level.
steps.description:
Following IT Security's instructions, Alice opens Windows Settings to install the critical security update that has been pending for 3 days.

This is how OS patches are actually installed: through your operating system's update settings, not through the EDR portal.
steps.instructions: Open the Settings app from the taskbar.

steps.name: Reporting the Incident
steps.description:
With the patch installed, the vulnerability is now closed. But this isn't over: Alice's credentials may have been compromised, suspicious login attempts are happening right now, and the IT Security team needs a full incident report.

This is no longer just a "blocked threat" to acknowledge. Real damage may have occurred, and the security team needs every detail to investigate and protect the organization.
steps.instructions: Open the EDR portal and click 'Report Incident'.

steps.name: Filing the Report

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue:
I received an email with a spreadsheet attachment titled Q3_Budget_Summary.xlsm. When I opened it and enabled macros, the EDR system detected a malicious process (svchost_update.exe) that accessed LSASS credential memory for approximately 4 seconds before being terminated.

The alert status was 'Partially Blocked': my credentials may have been exposed. I subsequently received an alert from IT Security about suspicious login attempts on my account from IP 185.234.xx.xx (Eastern Europe).

I have installed the pending security update KB5035853 via Windows Settings to close the vulnerability. The original email appeared to come from a colleague but was likely spoofed.

steps.description: Alice fills out the incident report form. This time, the report carries real weight: she's not just reporting a blocked threat, but a partial credential compromise with active exploitation attempts.
steps.instructions: Complete the incident report with details about the credential exposure and suspicious login attempts.

steps.name: IT Security Response

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thank you for your detailed report and swift action installing the security update. Here are our investigation findings:

Credential Impact:
  • Your credentials have been force-reset as a precaution: you will be prompted to create a new password at next login
  • The attacker kept trying your partially harvested credentials for about 4 minutes before we blocked the suspicious IP
  • None of those attempts signed in, but monitoring will continue for 30 days
Investigation Findings:
  • This was a targeted phishing campaign against our Finance department
  • 7 other employees received similar emails, and we are contacting them now
  • The sender address was spoofed to appear as an internal colleague
  • The attack exploited vulnerability CVE-2024-26169, which your missing patch (KB5035853, pending 3 days) left open
Root Cause:

Had KB5035853 been installed when it was released 3 days ago, the macro would still have run, but it would have hit a wall: without the elevation-of-privilege vulnerability it could never have reached credential memory. EDR would still have flagged the attempt, and the passwords held in system memory would have stayed out of reach.

Key Lessons:
  • Install security patches within 24-48 hours of release
  • A "Partially Blocked" alert means real damage may have occurred
  • Always report incidents, even partial blocks: your report helped us protect 7 other employees
  • Verify unexpected attachments, even from known contacts
Thank you for your vigilance. The combination of EDR detection and your quick reporting limited what could have been a much larger breach.

IT Security Team
email.subject: Re: EDR Alert Investigation, Credential Reset & Findings

highlighterTexts: The fallout is real: Alice's password is force-reset, and the attacker tried her partially harvested credentials before IT blocked the IP.
7 other employees got the same lure. Alice's report is what let IT warn them, so reporting even a partial block matters.
The root cause is the patch left pending for 3 days. With it installed, the macro could never have reached credential memory.

steps.description: Shortly after submitting the report, Alice receives a detailed response from the IT Security team. The investigation has revealed the full scope of the incident.
steps.instructions: Read the email from IT Security.

steps.name: Understanding EDR and Patching
steps.note: EDR and patching work together. EDR detects threats; patches remove the vulnerabilities those threats exploit. Without both, gaps remain.
steps.description:
Now that the incident is resolved, Alice reflects on what happened and what she's learned.

Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) is a security solution that continuously monitors your workstation for threats. How EDR Works:
  • Behavioral Analysis: Monitors process behavior, not just known malware signatures
  • Real-time Detection: Identifies suspicious activity as it happens
  • Automated Response: Can block threats automatically before damage occurs
  • Forensic Data: Records activity for investigation and learning
What Alice Learned the Hard Way: EDR is powerful, but it's not a safety net for skipped patches. In Alice's case, EDR detected the attack and killed the malicious process, but because the vulnerability existed (unpatched for 3 days), the attacker had a 4-second window to access credential memory. Those 4 seconds led to:
  • Partially harvested credentials
  • Suspicious login attempts from Eastern Europe
  • A forced credential reset for Alice
  • An investigation affecting 7 other employees
The Lesson: EDR catches attacks, but patches take away the weaknesses they rely on. A patched system + EDR = far less exposure: the macro would still have run with Alice's own rights, but it could not have reached credential memory. Best Practice: Install security updates within 24-48 hours of release. Critical patches should be installed immediately via Windows Settings.
steps.instructions: Click Next to review the key takeaways.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Congratulations on completing this training! Here are the key lessons from Alice's experience:
  • "Partially Blocked" means real consequences: Don't assume EDR handled everything. Review alert details carefully for signs of partial compromise
  • Delayed patches have real costs: 3 days of a pending patch led to credential exposure, suspicious login attempts, and a forced password reset
  • Install updates via Windows Settings: EDR monitors patch status, but updates are installed through your operating system settings, not the EDR portal
  • Report every incident with full details: Alice's detailed report helped IT Security identify and protect 7 other targeted employees
  • Verify unexpected attachments: Even files from known contacts could be malicious phishing attempts
  • Never enable macros blindly: Only enable macros in documents from trusted, verified sources
  • Patches + EDR work together: EDR catches threats in real time, and patches close the vulnerabilities attacks rely on. Neither is complete protection on its own
